h1: Deferred Adjudication & Defensive Driving for El Paso Tickets
intro: Deferred disposition and a driving safety course are the two tools Texas law gives a court to end a traffic ticket without a conviction. Attorney Robert Navar requests the right one for your case — and argues for it when the court is reluctant — for a flat fee from $59.
summary: Deferred disposition (often called deferred adjudication) under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45.051 means you pay a court fee, stay violation-free for 90–180 days, and the ticket is dismissed with no conviction.

A driving safety course dismissal under art. 45.0511 requires a 6-hour defensive driving course and a copy of your driving record; it is not available for speeds 25+ mph over, CDL holders, school-zone tickets in some courts, or if you used it in the last 12 months.
Both paths end with no conviction, no points and nothing for your insurer to rate — but asking for them yourself is a plea that gives up every other defense.
Having a lawyer request deferral keeps a dismissal on the table first and gets better terms from courts that refuse high-speed, repeat or CDL cases.
Flat fees: $59 in El Paso Municipal Court, $69 in JP, Horizon City, Socorro and the smaller city courts. Hire online or call 915-503-1600.

sections.heading: Deferred Disposition Under Article 45.051: How It Works
paragraphs: Deferred disposition is the Class C version of probation. Under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45.051, the judge accepts a plea of guilty or no contest but does not enter a judgment. Instead the court sets a deferral period — El Paso courts commonly use 90 to 180 days — and conditions that usually include a special expense fee (typically about the amount of the fine) and sometimes a driving safety course. If you complete the period, the case is dismissed. No conviction is reported to DPS, no points are assessed, and your insurance company has nothing to rate.

"Violation-free" is the condition that trips people up. It means no new traffic citation that results in a conviction during the period, anywhere in Texas, not just in the court that granted the deferral. A second ticket during the period can cause the judge to revoke the deferral and enter the original conviction.

sections.heading: Defensive Driving Under Article 45.0511: Eligibility and Costs
paragraphs: The driving safety course dismissal under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45.0511 is the other route. A qualifying driver asks the court for permission, completes a state-approved six-hour defensive driving course (online courses run about $25), obtains a certified Texas driving record, pays the court's administrative fee, and files everything within the time set — usually 90 days. The ticket is then dismissed. Our post on defensive driving in El Paso covers providers and paperwork.

Eligibility is narrower than for deferral. The statute and local practice exclude drivers who were cited for 25 mph or more over the limit, drivers who hold a commercial driver's license (even if they were in a personal car), drivers who have used the course for a dismissal in the past 12 months, and in some El Paso courts drivers cited for speeding in a school zone. For an eligible first-time driver with a modest speed, the course is often the cheapest path; for anyone outside those lines, deferral or a negotiated reduction is the plan.

sections.heading: When El Paso Courts Refuse Deferral or Defensive Driving
paragraphs: A judge is never required to grant deferred disposition. El Paso County judges typically refuse it, or offer it only with extra conditions, for speeds 25 mph or more over the limit, for drivers with several recent convictions, for school-zone and construction-zone tickets, and for anyone whose record shows a prior deferral revoked for a new violation. CDL holders are a special case: federal rules forbid a court from masking a CDL holder's conviction, so neither deferral nor the course is available to a commercial driver for a moving violation in any vehicle.

Those refusals are where a lawyer changes the outcome. A self-represented driver who is turned down for deferral has usually already entered a plea and is left with a conviction. When we appear, we can argue the request on the record, offer a longer period or an added course as a sweetener, or shift to a different result entirely — a reduction to a non-moving violation such as a defective-equipment charge, which carries no points and is not rated by insurers.

sections.heading: Why Having a Lawyer Request It Beats Asking Yourself
paragraphs: Every El Paso court lets a driver request deferred disposition or defensive driving on their own, by mail or at the clerk's window. The catch is that the request is a plea of guilty or no contest. The moment you make it, the court stops looking at whether the citation was defective, whether the officer could prove the speed, or whether the case should simply be dismissed. You also take the court's standard terms, with no one to argue for a different result if the judge says no.

Robert Navar's office does it in the opposite order. We file an appearance and a not-guilty plea, review the citation for grounds for an outright dismissal, and present those to the prosecutor at pretrial. Only if a dismissal is not available do we ask for deferral or the course, and we ask with the leverage of a case that could still go to trial. The practical difference for most clients is a dismissal instead of a deferral, or a deferral with better terms, for a flat $59 to $69 fee. You do not have to appear; we handle the docket and send you the order with instructions.

sections.heading: What Deferral Means for DPS, Insurance and Your Record
paragraphs: When a deferral is completed and the case dismissed, DPS receives no conviction, no points are added toward the four-in-12-months or seven-in-24-months suspension thresholds, and your driving record shows nothing from the stop. Insurers rate from the driving record, so a completed deferral is invisible to them. The court's own file still reflects the citation and the deferral order; drivers who want that cleared may be eligible for an expunction of a Class C deferred disposition after completion under Code of Criminal Procedure Chapter 55A.

sections.heading: What to Do Before You Ask the Court for Anything
paragraphs: Do not pay the ticket, do not mail in a defensive-driving request, and do not plead at the window. Note the appearance date and the issuing agency, then hire us online or call 915-503-1600. Tell us if you hold a CDL, used a course in the last year, or were in a school zone — each changes the plan. faqs.q: Is deferred adjudication the same as deferred disposition for a traffic ticket?
faqs.a: For Class C tickets the correct term is deferred disposition under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45.051, though many people and some courts call it deferred adjudication. Either way, it means a short violation-free period followed by a dismissal with no conviction.

faqs.q: How long is the deferral period in El Paso?
faqs.a: El Paso Municipal Court and most area courts set 90 to 180 days depending on the charge and the driver's record. The case is dismissed once the period ends without a new violation and the fee is paid.

faqs.q: Can I take defensive driving if I was going 25 over?
faqs.a: No. The driving safety course dismissal is not available for speeds 25 mph or more over the limit. Those cases call for deferred disposition or a negotiated reduction, which courts grant more readily when an attorney asks.

faqs.q: Does a completed deferral show up on my driving record or affect insurance?
faqs.a: No. A completed deferral is a dismissal; DPS receives no conviction, no points are added and insurers see nothing. The court's own records still show the citation, which an expunction can address if you want.

faqs.q: What happens if I get another ticket during the deferral period?
faqs.a: The court can revoke the deferral and enter a conviction on the original charge. If that happens, call us right away — the new ticket can often be handled so that it does not become a conviction before the deferral ends.

faqs.q: Why not just request deferred disposition myself and save the fee?
faqs.a: Because the request is a guilty plea that ends any chance of an outright dismissal, and the court can simply say no, leaving you with a conviction. For $59–$69 we look for a dismissal first, then request deferral with leverage.
